content: An environment should be established to facilitate the adoption of this recommendation, which includes promoting behavioral changes among healthcare practitioners to support evidence-based practices. In humanitarian emergencies, the adaptation of recommendations must align with and integrate into other response strategies. Special attention should be given to the unique needs of women in emergency settings, considering their values and preferences. Additionally, context-specific tools and toolkits may be necessary, alongside standard tools, to aid stakeholders in implementing this updated recommendation in humanitarian contexts. The successful integration of this recommendation into national programs and health services requires well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes for adaptation and implementation. This may involve developing or revising existing national guidelines or protocols. Recommendations should be tailored into documents and tools suitable for various locations and contexts to address the specific needs of each country and health service. Any modifications to the recommendation must be explicitly justified and transparently communicated. An enabling environment should also include education initiatives to encourage behavior change among skilled health personnel providing care during childbirth, ensuring the use of evidence-based practices. To implement this recommendation effectively, several considerations must be addressed. Healthcare workers in antenatal care settings require training and supportive supervision to perform dating ultrasounds. Additionally, health professionals need training to counsel women on the benefits and side effects of different labor induction methods. Women should be adequately informed and involved in shared decision-making regarding the indications and methods for labor induction. In lowand middle-income countries, healthcare worker shortages may result in staff attending to significantly higher numbers of women in labor wards compared to other settings. This can challenge the provision of adequate support, assessment, and monitoring, potentially reducing the capacity of health workers to respond promptly to emergencies. Furthermore, a higher proportion of labor inductions are attended by medical doctors compared to non-induced deliveries, which has implications for the distribution and productivity of medical professionals, particularly in resource-limited settings. Safe labor induction requires the availability of appropriate medicines, mechanical devices, monitoring equipment, and access to facilities for safe cesarean sections. Inconsistent supply or lack of these resources, as well as inadequate facilities, may pose challenges in some settings. The WHO has identified evidence gaps regarding outpatient labor induction, particularly in determining its suitability for women in high-income versus lowand middle-income countries. Large, randomized studies are needed to assess the safety and acceptability of outpatient versus inpatient labor induction. If safety is comparable, the most effective method (e.g., Foley catheter or low-dose misoprostol) should be evaluated. Research should also differentiate between unsupervised home settings and semi-supervised environments, such as maternity waiting homes, during different phases of cervical ripening and labor induction. The implementation and impact of this recommendation will be monitored at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve maternal and newborn care quality. Data collection and evaluation at the country and regional levels will assess the recommendation’s impact on national policies. Local-level information can be obtained through interrupted time series or clinical audits. Suggested indicators include the proportion of pregnant women receiving ultrasounds before 24 weeks of gestation and the proportion with documented indications for labor induction. The WHO Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) reviews maternal and perinatal health recommendations annually to prioritize updates. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendation may be updated. Following publication and dissemination, any concerns about the recommendation’s validity will be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans for updates. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates.
